                                 PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                       §
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY                        §
LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION                        §                     BEFORE THE
SERVICE CORPORATION TO                           §
AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF                      §
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY                        §                   STATE OFFICE OF
FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST                         §
SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION                    §
765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE                         §
PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,                         §
CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,                       §
LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH,                         §                   ADMINISTRATIVE
MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN                        §                     HEARINGS
SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,                     §
AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                          §


           DONALD LEE JOINER AND ANITA M. JOINERS’ INITIAL BRIEF

       Donald Lee Joiner and Anita M. Joiner (the “Joiners”) file this initial post-hearing brief

and would respectfully show the following:

                                       I.     SUMMARY

       The Joiners (Party 115) oppose certification of any route that includes Link E4, and

specifically oppose Routes 376, 381, and 382, the three filed routes that include Link E4. First, no

expert in this proceeding recommended Routes 376, 381, or 382, and every expert who ranked

routes placed them at or near the bottom. Second, Routes 376, 381, and 382 are among the ten

longest routes of the 132 filed alternatives. Third, Routes 376, 381, and 382 are among the ten to

thirteen most expensive routes in the docket. Indeed, the estimates do not include site-specific

design requirements or crossing-specific cost adders for Williamson County regulatory

compliance. None of the remaining criteria favor Routes 376, 381, or 382. The Commission should




                                                 1
 decline to certify any route that includes Link E4 and should certify Route 487, Route 894, or any

other C4 to D12 corridor route.

                                II.    STANDARD OF REVIEW

        This proceeding is a contested case before the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

The presiding administrative law judges will prepare a Proposal for Decision containing proposed

findings of fact and conclusions of law, which the Commission may adopt, modify, or reject. Tex.

Gov’t Code Ann. § 2001.058(e) (West 2008 & Supp. 2014). The applicable legal standard is PURA

§ 37.056(a), which requires a finding that the certificate is necessary for the service,

accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public, and PURA § 37.056(c), which directs

consideration of community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and

other applicable criteria. Tex. Util. Code Ann. § 37.056(a), (c) (West 2007 & Supp. 2014) (PURA).

The Commission’s rules elaborate the routing factors at 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

(TAC). The burden of demonstrating that the proposed route meets the statutory and regulatory

criteria rests with the applicants.

         III.    THE ROUTES THAT USE LINK E4, ROUTES 376, 381, AND 382,
                          DO NOT MEET PUC CRITERIA

A.      No expert recommended Routes 376, 381, or 382, and every expert who ranked

routes placed them at or near the bottom.

        The expert record is uniformly adverse to Routes 376, 381, and 382. Commission Staff’s

witness John Poole evaluated all 132 filed routes and recommends Route 487. Direct Testimony

of John Pool, Staff Ex. 1 at 29. On habitable structures within 500 feet of the centerline, Route 376

ties for the highest count in the entire docket at 122 structures; Routes 381 and 382 carry 107 and

108 structures, respectively. Staff Ex. 1 at 61. On cost, Routes 381, 376, and 382 rank among the

most expensive of 132 routes; only ten to twelve routes cost more. Staff Ex. 1 at 51. On right-of-


                                                 2
 way corridor use, Routes 376, 381, and 382 parallel compatible rights-of-way for only 39.75,

41.30, and 42.62 percent of their length – near the bottom of the 132-route field. Staff Ex. 1 at 57–

58. Route 487, by contrast, parallels compatible rights-of-way for 49.64 percent of its length, the

4th highest of any route. Staff Ex. 1 at 65.

       Brian C. Andrews ranked Route 376 last, 122nd of 122, in his seven-factor composite

analysis, with Routes 381 and 382 at 107th and 108th. Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews,

Hodge-Schwertner Ex. 1 at 23, Ex. BCA-3. James W. Daniel designated Link B3 as

“unacceptable,” and every filed route that includes Link E4 contains Link B3 in the B3-E3-E4

sequence. Direct Testimony of James W. Daniel, Theon-Voss Exh. 1 at 10; Theon-Voss Exh. 2 at

2; App. D, Tbl. 7-1. Daniel’s table places Route 894, the C4 to D12 route with no Link B3, E3, or

E4, as row one, labeled “None – Best Fit.” Id. Joshua Rhodes and Mark Turnbough each

recommended routes from corridors that avoid Link E4. Direct Testimony of Joshua Rhodes,

Solana Ex. 4 at 18–19; Direct Testimony of Mark Turnbough, BCI Ex. 4 at 20. Casey D. Petty, the

applicants’ routing witness, identified Route 894 as the route that best addresses PURA and the

Commission’s rules. Petty’s rebuttal testimony confirms that each expert who expressed a route

preference: Daniel, Andrews, Anderson, Buntz, and others supports Route 894 or Route 487, not

any route that includes Link E4. Rebuttal Testimony of Casey D. Petty, Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex.

13 at 3–4. The Joiners are not aware of any expert who recommended Routes 376, 381, or 382.

B.     Routes 376, 381, and 382 are among the longest and most expensive routes in the

docket.

       Route 376 is 1,256,384 feet long, approximately the 8th longest of 132 routes. Routes 382

(1,255,583 feet) and 381 (1,252,326 feet) are nearly as long. Only about seven or eight routes in

the entire field are longer than Route 376. Staff Ex. 1 at 54–58. Staff’s recommended Route 487



                                                 3
 is 1,169,505 feet, the 43rd shortest route, roughly 87,000 feet shorter than Route 376. Id. at 39.

Oncor’s Route 894 is also substantially shorter. Routes 376, 381, and 382 are not marginally longer

than a handful of alternatives; they are near the outer edge of the length distribution across all 132

filed routes. Id.

        The cost picture mirrors the length picture. Routes 381 ($2,158,457,000), 376

($2,160,048,000), and 382 ($2,164,269,000) rank among the thirteen most expensive of 132

routes; only ten to twelve routes cost more. Staff Ex. 1 at 51. Route 487 costs $2,060,282,000

(22nd least expensive), roughly $100 million less than Route 376, and Route 894 costs

$2,076,387,000. Id. at 49, 51.

C.      Link E4 fails the specific routing criteria.

        1.      Corridor parallelism.

        Link E4 runs zero feet parallel to any existing transmission line, railroad, public road, or

pipeline. Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, p. 1759 (App. E, Tbl. 7-3 at 3). Total parallel to compatible

rights-of-way is only 6,328 feet, or about 23.8 percent of the link’s length. Id. Oncor removed Link

J5 from the project because it did not follow road corridors and property boundaries; it chose a

modified Link J6 that follows FM 501 and apparent property boundaries as the lower impact

alternative. The corridor parallelism deficit that eliminated Link J5 is present, and worse, in Link

E4.

        2.      Property lines.

        Link E4 parallels apparent property boundaries for only 5,502 feet of its 26,569-foot

length—about 20.7 percent. Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, p. 1759 (App. E, Tbl. 7-3 at 3). Oncor

admits the figures are based on tax parcel data and that “individual parcels may not represent the

full extent of a landowner’s contiguous property holdings.” The Joiners own Tract 2665 and Tract



                                                  4
 2680 as separate tax parcels but operate them as a single contiguous farm held in the family since

the early 1900s. Joiner Ex. 1 at 6–7. Link E4 runs along the internal boundary between those two

tracts, through the middle of the working farm. Id. at 7–8. By Oncor’s own routing framework,

which disfavors links that “cut through numerous smaller parcels, resulting in increased property

and habitat fragmentation,” Link E4 fails.

       3.      Prudent avoidance.

       Route 376 ties for the highest habitable structure count in the docket: 122 structures within

500 feet of the centerline. Staff Ex. 1 at 61. Routes 381 and 382 carry 107 and 108. Id. Link E4

passes between two family homes on the Joiner farm: Habitable Structure 112, the Beyer/Joiner

family home built in 1900, sitting 350 feet east of the centerline, and the 2016 Joiner home

designated in the Joiners’ estate plan for their daughter Kathleen, sitting approximately 600 feet

west. Joiner Ex. 1 at 8, 15–16.

       4.      Williamson County regulatory exposure.

       Link E4 enters Williamson County and triggers the Corps of Engineers Regional Condition

1 to Nationwide Permit 57, requiring a Pre Construction Notification for activities in Karst Zones

1 and 2 in Williamson County, and the TCEQ Edwards Aquifer Protection Program, which

imposes preconstruction approval requirements under 30 TAC ch. 213. Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex.

1, p. 226-27. A route staying in Bell County on the C4 to D12 corridor triggers neither.

Approximately 5,092 feet of Link E4 also runs through areas of high archaeological or historical

site potential, including the Joiner family farm held continuously since the early 1900s. Oncor &

LCRA TSC Ex. 1, p. 1758 (App. E, Tbl. 7-3 at 3); Joiner Ex. 1 at 15–17.




                                                5
 D.     The Commission must find Link E4 specifically necessary; Route 894 and Route 487

are superior on every measure.

       The Commission is not required to certify any route that was filed and not required to

accept any route simply because no alternative is perfect. The applicants admit they do not have a

preferred route and that the process narrowing 1,246 evaluated routes to 122 filed routes “was not

to select a best meets route, but rather to reduce the total number of proposed routes” to meet

geographic diversity requirements. Route 894 and Route 487 each use the C4 to D12 corridor, stay

in Bell County, avoid Link E4 and its Williamson County regulatory exposure, and are shorter and

less expensive than Routes 376, 381, and 382. Every expert in the record who expressed a

preference identified Route 894, Route 487, or another C4 to D12 alternative as superior. No

conceivable balancing of the statutory routing factors supports certifying Routes 376, 381, or 382

over these alternatives. The Commission should decline to certify any route that includes Link E4.

                    IV.     CONCLUSION AND RELIEF REQUESTED

       For the reasons above, the Joiners respectfully request that the Commission decline to

certify any route that includes Link E4. The Joiners support, in the alternative, certification of

Route 894 or any other route that uses the C4 to D12 corridor, which Oncor has identified as the

route that best addresses the requirements of PURA and the Commission’s Substantive Rules and

which avoids the corridor parallelism deficits, the property line deficits, the prudent avoidance

burden on a century old family home, the karst zone PCN trigger, the Edwards Aquifer Protection

Program exposure, and the federally listed species habitat impacts that come with Link E4 and the

Williamson County entry. The Joiners support certification of Route 487, Route 894, or any other

route from the C4 to D12 corridor.




                                                6
                                              Respectfully submitted,

                                             NATHAN WESELY PLLC

docket on June 19, 2026.
